p.src: Now Sun the Great Sage, having recovered his golden-hooped staff, fought his way out through the entrance, leapt onto the high peak, and joyfully rejoined the assembled gods. Heavenly King Li asked, “How did you fare this time?” The Pilgrim replied, “Old Sun transformed himself and slipped into his cave, only to find the monster singing and dancing more merrily than ever as he drank his victory wine. I still could not discover where he kept his treasure. When I went around to the rear, I suddenly heard horses neighing and dragons roaring, and knew they were the possessions of the Fire Department. My golden-hooped staff was leaning against the eastern wall. Old Sun seized it, and fought his way out with it in hand.” The gods said, “You have recovered your treasure, but when will ours be restored to us?” The Pilgrim replied, “That will not be difficult, not difficult at all. Now that I have this iron staff, whatever it takes, I shall strike him down, recover your treasures, and return them to you.”

p.src: While they were still speaking, gongs and drums suddenly sounded together below the hillside, and battle cries shook the earth. It was King Rhinoceros leading his host of spirits in pursuit of the Pilgrim. When the Pilgrim saw them, he cried, “Good, good, good! This is exactly what I wanted. Please remain seated, gentlemen, while Old Sun goes to capture him once more.” What a Great Sage! Raising his iron staff, he charged straight at the monster and shouted, “Where do you think you are going, vile demon? Taste my staff!” The monster blocked the blow with his spear and cursed, “Thieving monkey! You are utterly outrageous. How dare you rob me of my possessions in broad daylight?” The Pilgrim replied, “You doomed brute! You used that ring of yours to seize my property in broad daylight, yet which of those things belonged to you? Do not run—take a blow from your lord!” The monster whirled his spear to parry the blow. A splendid battle followed:

p.src: The demon king and Sun the Great Sage fought for three double-hours without either gaining the victory, until once again the sky was growing dark. Bracing himself behind his long spear, the demon said, “Wukong, hold! Heaven and earth are dark; this is no time for a contest. Let us both rest awhile and resume our match tomorrow morning.” The Pilgrim cursed, “Silence, vile brute! Old Sun is only now getting into his stride. What do I care if night is falling? I shall not stop until victory and defeat are settled between us.” The monster gave a shout, made a feint with his spear, and fled for his life. He led the demons in withdrawing their weapons, entered the cave, and barred its gate tightly shut.

p.src: The Great Sage dragged his staff back, and the heavenly gods at the bank congratulated him, all saying, “Truly this mighty and powerful Great Sage Equaling Heaven possesses immeasurable skill.” The Pilgrim laughed and said, “You flatter me, you flatter me.” Heavenly King Li stepped forward and said, “These words are no mere flattery. You truly are a splendid champion. This battle was no less magnificent than when you once concealed yourself from the earth-net and the heaven-snare.” The Pilgrim said, “Let us say no more of old affairs. After the fight Old Sun gave him, that demon must certainly be weary. I cannot afford to complain of fatigue either. All of you sit at ease while I enter the cave again and discover the secret of his ring. I must steal it from him, capture the monster, recover your weapons, and return them to you so that you may ascend to Heaven.” The prince said, “It is already night. Would it not be better to sleep here and go tomorrow morning?” The Pilgrim laughed. “You young fellow know nothing of the world. When have you ever seen a thief choose broad daylight to ply his trade? Such pilfering must be done by night, coming and going without anyone noticing. That is the proper way to conduct the business.” Lord Fire Virtue and the Thunder Duke said, “Third Prince, say no more. We understand nothing of such business. The Great Sage is an old hand who knows every trick of the trade. Let him seize this opportunity: first, the demon is weary; second, the night is dark and he will be off his guard. Please go quickly, quickly!”

p.src: Stretching out his long legs, he made three or five bounds to the gate, squeezed through a crack, and crouched at the foot of the wall, carefully observing the interior by the lamplight. He saw the whole company of demons, great and small, devouring their food like wolves and tigers. The Pilgrim chirped and trilled like a cricket for a while. Before long they put away the household utensils, then went to prepare their sleeping places and each settled down for the night.

p.src: At about the first watch, the Pilgrim reached a room at the rear. He heard the old demon issue an order: “Let the guards at every gate sleep lightly, lest Sun Wukong transform himself into something else, slip into our home, and steal from us.” There were also guards assigned to the night watch; they made a noisy commotion as clappers and bells sounded together. This made it all the easier for the Great Sage to act. He slipped through the bedroom door and saw a stone bed. On either side stood several mountain spirits and tree demons with powdered faces and rouged cheeks. They spread the bedding and waited upon the old demon, some removing his footwear and others undressing him. When the demon king loosened his clothes, the Pilgrim saw the gleaming white ring encircling his left upper arm; it looked like a bracelet of linked pearls. Rather than remove it, he pushed it twice farther up his arm, securing it tightly before lying down. Seeing this, the Pilgrim transformed himself again, this time into a yellow flea. He leapt onto the stone bed, burrowed beneath the covers, crawled onto the monster’s arm, and bit him hard. The sting made the monster roll over and curse, “You wretched servants, you need a beating! You neither shook out the quilt nor swept the bed. Something has just bitten me!” He pushed the ring twice farther up his arm and lay down again. The Pilgrim crawled onto the ring and bit him once more. Unable to sleep, the monster rolled over again and cried, “This itching is tormenting me to death!”

p.src: The Pilgrim saw that the monster was tightly guarded and kept the treasure on his person, refusing to remove it, so he concluded that it could not be stolen. He jumped down from the bed, changed back into a cricket, left the room, and went straight to the rear, where once again he heard dragons roaring and horses neighing. The inner gate was securely locked, and the fire dragons and fire horses were tethered inside. The Pilgrim resumed his true form and approached the gate. Employing a lock-opening spell, he recited the incantation and swept his hand across the lock. With a sharp clack, both bolts sprang free. He pushed open the gate and burst in to look around. The fire implements within shone so brilliantly that the place was as bright as day. He suddenly noticed several weapons leaning at an angle against the eastern and western sides. They included the prince’s demon-cleaving saber and other arms, as well as Lord Fire Virtue’s fire bow, fire arrows, and the rest of his equipment. By the firelight, the Pilgrim inspected the whole place. Then he saw a small bamboo tray on a stone table behind the gate, with a handful of fine hairs lying upon it. The Great Sage was overjoyed. He picked up the hairs, breathed two warm breaths upon them, and cried, “Change!” They instantly transformed into thirty or fifty little monkeys. He ordered them to carry away all the confiscated items: sabers, swords, pestles, cords, spiked wheels, bows, arrows, spears, carts, gourds, fire crows, fire rats, and fire horses. Then he mounted the fire dragon, unleashed the flames, and began burning outward from within. A roaring and crackling, banging and crashing filled the air, just like a succession of thunderclaps and cannon blasts. The demons, great and small, were startled from their befuddled dreams. Wrapped in quilts and with their heads covered, some shouted and others wept. Every one of them found all escape cut off, and more than half were burned to death by the flames. By the time the Handsome Monkey King returned in triumph, it was about the third watch of the night.

p.src: Now on the lofty peak, Heavenly King Li and the others suddenly saw the blaze flare brightly and all rushed forward together. They saw Pilgrim riding the dragon, shouting and hollering as he drove the little monkeys straight up to the summit, where he cried in a stern voice, “Come and reclaim your weapons! Come and reclaim your weapons!” Lord Fire Virtue and Nezha answered him. Pilgrim shook himself, and all those hairs returned to his body. Prince Nezha retrieved his six weapons, while Lord Fire Virtue ordered the gods of the Fire Ministry to recover the fire dragons and the rest. All smiled and congratulated Pilgrim, but we shall say no more of that.

p.src: Meanwhile, flames raged throughout Golden-Cincture Cave, frightening the Great King Rhinoceros nearly out of his wits. He hurriedly rose, opened his chamber door, and, holding the ring in both hands, thrust it eastward and the eastern fires died, thrust it westward and the western fires vanished. Amid smoke and leaping flames that filled the air, he ran all around with the treasure until every fire in every quarter had been extinguished. He hastened to rescue and muster his demons, but more than half had already burned to death; males and females together, he could gather scarcely more than a hundred. When he inspected the armory, he found every weapon gone. He then went to look in the rear and saw that Bajie, Sha Monk, and the elder remained bound and had not escaped; the White Dragon Horse was still at its manger, and the luggage was still inside the building. The fiend said bitterly, “Some careless little demon must have let a fire break out and brought this disaster upon us.” A close attendant beside him reported, “Great King, this fire had nothing to do with anyone of our household. It was most likely the work of a thief who slipped into our camp, released the creatures of the Fire Ministry, and stole away the divine weapons.” Only then did the old fiend understand. “It could be no one else. It must have been that rogue Sun Wukong. No wonder I could not rest easily when I went to sleep. That thieving monkey must have transformed himself and slipped inside, then bitten my arm twice. He surely meant to steal my treasure, but found it cinched too tightly to lay hands on; so instead he stole the weapons, released the fire dragons, and carried out this vicious scheme in hopes of burning me to death. You thieving monkey! You have wasted all your cunning, for you know nothing of my powers. So long as I carry this treasure, I could enter the great ocean without drowning or plunge into a pool of fire without burning. If I catch that rogue this time, nothing short of scraping his flesh from his bones and chopping it into pieces will satisfy me.”

p.src: After saying this, he fretted for a long while, until before he knew it the cock crowed and dawn broke. On the high peak, once the prince had recovered his six weapons, he said to Pilgrim, “Great Sage, daylight has come. We must not delay. Let us take advantage of the fiend’s shaken spirits: with the Fire Ministry and the others assisting you, we shall go and fight him again. Perhaps this time we can capture him.” Pilgrim laughed. “That makes good sense. Let us unite our hearts and go have some sport.” Each displayed his formidable bearing, eager to exercise his martial skill, and they went straight to the cave entrance. Pilgrim shouted, “Come out, you vile fiend, and fight Old Monkey!”

Suddenly seeing all the sages arrive together, they panicked, dropped their brooms and ash rakes, and ran inside to report once more, “Sun Wukong has brought a great many heavenly gods and is challenging us outside the gate again!” The Rhinoceros Fiend was greatly alarmed by the report; grinding his steel teeth with a harsh rasp, he rolled his ringed eyes and opened them wide. Leveling his long spear and carrying his treasure, he strode out through the entrance and unleashed a torrent of abuse: “You thieving monkey who raided my camp and set it ablaze! What powers do you possess that you dare hold me in such contempt?” Pilgrim replied with a smiling curse, “You vile monster! If you wish to know my powers, step forward and I shall tell you:

p.src: Hearing this, the monster pointed at Pilgrim and said, “So you are the great thief who once robbed Heaven. Do not run—take a thrust of my spear!” The Great Sage met him with his staff. While the two were locked in combat, Prince Nezha grew furious and Lord Fire Virtue turned fierce. At once they hurled the six divine weapons and the implements of the Fire Ministry at the fiend. The Great Sage Sun fought with still greater might. From another side the Lord of Thunder wielded his wedge and the Heavenly King raised his saber; all surged forward together without regard for rank or order. The fiend gave a lofty, cold laugh, secretly drew the treasure from his sleeve, tossed it into the air, and cried, “Take them!” With a great whoosh, it swept away once more all six divine weapons, the implements of the Fire Ministry, the Lord of Thunder’s wedge, the Heavenly King’s saber, and Pilgrim’s staff. The gods were left empty-handed as before, and the Great Sage Sun once again had only his bare fists. Victorious, the fiend turned back and called, “Little ones, carry stones and rebuild the gate! Break ground for repairs and put the chambers and galleries in order anew. When all is ready, we shall kill Tang Monk and his two disciples as an offering to the earth, then share the blessing and feast together.” The little demons received the order and set about the work, but we shall say no more of them.

p.src: Meanwhile, Heavenly King Li led the company back to the high peak. Lord Fire Virtue blamed Nezha for his impatience, and the Lord of Thunder faulted the Heavenly King for acting willfully; only the Lord of Waters stood silently beside them. Seeing that they would not even look at one another, Pilgrim was troubled at heart. Having no alternative, he hid his resentment behind forced cheer and said to them with a smile, “Gentlemen, there is no need to be distressed. As the old saying goes, ‘Victory and defeat are both common fortunes of war.’ When it comes to martial skill, he and I are merely evenly matched. It is only because he possesses that ring that he can cause such harm and has taken all our weapons away again. Set your minds at ease and let Old Monkey go investigate his origins once more.” The prince said, “You previously petitioned the Jade Emperor and investigated all the realms beneath Heaven, yet found not the slightest trace. Where can you investigate now?” Pilgrim replied, “It has occurred to me that the Buddha’s power knows no bounds. I shall now go west to ask my Buddha, the Tathagata, to survey the four continents of the earth with his wisdom eye and discover in what region this monster was born, where his native home and dwelling lie, and what manner of treasure that ring is. Whatever it takes, I shall capture him, avenge you gentlemen, and restore your good cheer before you return to Heaven.” The gods said, “If that is your intention, do not linger. Go quickly! Go quickly!”

p.src: As Pilgrim was admiring the mountain scenery, he suddenly heard someone call, “Sun Wukong, where have you come from? And where are you going?” He turned quickly and saw that it was the Venerable Bhikshuni. The Great Sage bowed and said, “There is a matter for which I wish to see the Tathagata.” The Bhikshuni said, “You mischievous creature! If you wish to see the Tathagata, why do you not enter the precious monastery instead of standing here admiring the mountain?” Pilgrim replied, “It is my first visit to this noble place, so I took the liberty.” The Bhikshuni said, “Come quickly and follow me.” Pilgrim followed closely to the gate of Thunderclap Monastery, where he saw the Eight Great Vajra Guardians standing in imposing ranks on either side and barring the way. The Bhikshuni said, “Wukong, wait here a moment while I go inside and report your arrival.” Pilgrim had no choice but to remain standing outside the gate. The Bhikshuni went before the Buddha, joined her palms, and said, “Sun Wukong has business here and wishes to see the Tathagata.” The Tathagata issued an order that he be admitted, and only then did the Vajra Guardians step aside and let him pass.

u.src: As Pilgrim was admiring the mountain scenery, he suddenly heard someone call, “Sun Wukong, where have you come from?
And where are you going?”
He turned quickly and saw that it was the Venerable Bhikshuni.
The Great Sage bowed and said, “There is a matter for which I wish to see the Tathagata.”
The Bhikshuni said, “You mischievous creature!
If you wish to see the Tathagata, why do you not enter the precious monastery instead of standing here admiring the mountain?”
Pilgrim replied, “It is my first visit to this noble place, so I took the liberty.”
The Bhikshuni said, “Come quickly and follow me.”
Pilgrim followed closely to the gate of Thunderclap Monastery, where he saw the Eight Great Vajra Guardians standing in imposing ranks on either side and barring the way.
The Bhikshuni said, “Wukong, wait here a moment while I go inside and report your arrival.”
Pilgrim had no choice but to remain standing outside the gate.
The Bhikshuni went before the Buddha, joined her palms, and said, “Sun Wukong has business here and wishes to see the Tathagata.”
The Tathagata issued an order that he be admitted, and only then did the Vajra Guardians step aside and let him pass.

p.src: When the Pilgrim had bowed his head in worship, the Tathagata asked, “Wukong, I heard that the Venerable Guanyin freed you and that you embraced the Buddhist faith and undertook to escort the Tang monk here to seek the scriptures. Why have you come here alone? What has happened?” The Pilgrim bowed his head to the ground and said, “I report to my Buddha: Since your disciple received the protection of the Buddhist Law, I have journeyed westward with my Tang master. When we reached Golden Pouch Mountain and Golden Pouch Cave, we encountered a wicked demon called Great King Rhinoceros, whose magic powers are immense. He swept my master and fellow disciples into his cave. I demanded them back, but he answered me with malice. We fought, and with a gleaming white ring he snatched away my iron staff. Fearing that he might be a heavenly general who had descended to the mortal world, I hurried up to Heaven to investigate, but found no trace of him. The Jade Emperor graciously dispatched Heavenly King Li and his sons to assist me, but the demon also snatched away the prince’s six weapons. Then I invited the Lord of the Fire Star to burn him with fire, but the demon took away all his fire implements as well. Next I asked the Lord of the Water Star to drown him with water, but not so much as a drop could touch him. After expending a great deal of spirit and strength, I stole back the iron staff and the other weapons. But when I challenged him again, he caught them all once more in his ring, and we had no means of subduing him. I have therefore come especially to report this to my Buddha. I beg you in your compassion to look into what manner of creature he truly is, so that I may seize his kin and neighbors, capture the demon, and rescue my master. With hands joined in reverence, I beseech you to bring our holy quest to fruition.”

p.src: Hearing this, the Tathagata gazed afar with his wisdom-eye and at once understood the truth. He said to the Pilgrim, “Though I know that monster, I cannot tell you about him. You, monkey, are loose-tongued. If word spreads that I exposed him, he will refuse to fight you, come clamoring up to Spirit Mountain, and bring trouble upon me instead. I shall send some magic power from here to help you capture him.” The Pilgrim bowed again in thanks and asked, “What magic power will the Tathagata lend me?” The Tathagata immediately ordered the eighteen venerable arhats to open the treasury, take out eighteen grains of cinnabar-gold sand, and lend their aid to Wukong. The Pilgrim asked, “What can this cinnabar-gold sand do?” The Tathagata replied, “Go outside the cave and challenge the demon to a contest. Lure him out, and then have the arhats cast down the sand. It will entrap him so that he can neither move his body nor pull free his feet, and you may seize and beat him as you please.” The Pilgrim laughed. “Wonderful, wonderful, wonderful! Let us go at once.”

p.src: The arhats dared not delay; they immediately fetched the cinnabar-gold sand and set out. The Pilgrim thanked the Tathagata once more. Looking over the company on the way, he saw only sixteen arhats and cried, “What sort of place is this, where men are allowed to slip away?” The arhats asked, “Who has slipped away?” The Pilgrim replied, “Eighteen were originally assigned, so why are there only sixteen now?” Before he had finished, the Dragon-Subduing and Tiger-Taming Arhats emerged from within and came forward, saying, “Wukong, why are you being so unreasonable already? We two stayed behind to hear the Tathagata’s instructions.” The Pilgrim said, “What airs you put on! What airs! If I had cried out even a little later, I daresay you would never have come out at all.” The arhats laughed merrily and mounted their auspicious clouds.

p.src: Before long, they reached the bounds of Golden Pouch Mountain. When Heavenly King Li saw them, he led the others forward to welcome them and gave a full account of what had happened. The arhats said, “There is no need for tedious details. Hurry and call him out.” The Great Sage clenched his fists, went to the mouth of the cave, and cursed, “You fat, insolent monster! Come out quickly and see which of us is superior—your Grandpa Sun or you!” One of the lesser demons again ran swiftly inside to report. The Demon King said angrily, “I wonder whom that thieving monkey has invited this time to help him run wild.” The lesser demon said, “There are no other generals—only he himself.” The Demon King said, “His staff has already been taken by me, so why has he come here alone again? Can he mean to fight with his fists?” Taking his treasure with him, he grasped his spear, ordered the lesser demons to move aside the stone blocks, and leapt out through the entrance. He cursed, “Thieving monkey! You have failed to gain the advantage time after time and ought to keep away. Why have you come shouting again?” The Pilgrim said, “You insolent demon cannot tell good from ill! If you want your grandpa to stop coming, you must submit, apologize, and send out my master and fellow disciples. Then I shall spare you.” The monster said, “Those three monks of yours have already been washed clean and will soon be slaughtered. Do you still not understand the situation? Be gone!”

Abandoning all formal stance, he swung his fist, advanced obliquely with a hooking step, and aimed a blow at the demon’s face; the monster thrust out his long spear and met the blow head-on. The Pilgrim leapt left and right, enticing the demon after him; unaware that this was a ruse, the demon pursued him southward away from the cave entrance. The Pilgrim at once signaled the arhats, who all cast their cinnabar-gold sand down upon the demon. What marvelous sand! Indeed:

p.src: The demon saw the flying sand obscure his eyes. He lowered his head for an instant, and the sand beneath his feet was already more than three feet deep. In alarm, he sprang upward and landed atop the rising layer. Before he could stand firm, in a moment the sand had risen more than another two feet. The monster grew desperate. Pulling his feet free, he hurriedly took out his ring, tossed it upward, and cried, “Catch!” With a tremendous whoosh, the ring caught all eighteen grains of cinnabar-gold sand. The monster wheeled around and went straight back to his cave.

p.src: One by one, the arhats halted their clouds with empty hands. The Pilgrim approached and asked, “Venerable arhats, why have you stopped casting the sand?” The arhats replied, “There was a sudden noise just now, and the cinnabar-gold sand vanished.” The Pilgrim laughed. “That thing of his has caught it again.” Heavenly King Li and the others said, “If he is so difficult to subdue, how are we ever to capture him? When shall we return to Heaven, and with what face can we appear before the Emperor?” Standing nearby, the Dragon-Subduing and Tiger-Taming Arhats said to the Pilgrim, “Wukong, do you know why the two of us were delayed in setting out?” The Pilgrim replied, “Old Sun merely blamed you for hiding away and refusing to come. I did not know you had something to tell me.” The arhats said, “The Tathagata instructed us: ‘That demon possesses immense magic power. If the cinnabar-gold sand is lost, tell Sun Wukong to go to the Tushita Palace in the Heaven of Parting Sorrow and seek his trail from the Supreme Lord Lao. Then perhaps the demon may be captured in a single assault.’” Hearing this, the Pilgrim said, “How vexing! How vexing! The Tathagata has played a trick on Old Sun too. He should have told me at once. Then you would not have had to make this long journey.” Heavenly King Li said, “Since the Tathagata has given this clear direction, Great Sage, you should set out without delay.”

p.src: Good Monkey! Saying he was off, he sprang onto a somersault cloud and flew straight through the Southern Gate of Heaven. The Four Great Marshals were there and greeted him with clasped hands, asking, “How goes the capture of the monster?” As he hurried on, the Monkey replied, “Not yet, not yet. Now I have somewhere to seek its origin.” The four commanders dared not detain him and let him pass through the heavenly gate. He went neither to the Hall of Divine Mists nor to the Palace of the Dipper and Bull, but headed directly beyond the Thirty-three Heavens to the Tushita Palace in the Heaven of Dissolving Hatred. Seeing two immortal lads standing in attendance, he gave neither name nor introduction and strode straight in. The two lads hurriedly caught hold of him and said, “Who are you? Where are you going?” Only then did the Monkey say, “I am the Great Sage Equal to Heaven, and I have come to find Lord Lao.” The immortal lads said, “Why are you so rude? Wait here and let us announce you.” The Monkey would hear none of it. With a shout, he strode straight inside. Suddenly Lord Lao came out from within, and the two ran squarely into each other. The Monkey bowed and greeted him, saying, “Old sir, it has been a long time.” Lord Lao laughed. “Why has this monkey come here instead of fetching the scriptures?” The Monkey said, “Fetching scriptures, fetching scriptures—we have not stopped by day or night. But we met with an obstacle, so I have come here on an errand.” Lord Lao said, “What have obstructions on the road to the Western Heaven to do with me?” The Monkey said, “Western Heaven or no, say no more. Once I find the trail, I shall have the matter out with you.” Lord Lao said, “This is the supreme palace of immortals. What trail could there be for you to find?”

p.src: The Monkey went inside, staring intently and looking all around. After passing through several galleries and halls, he suddenly saw a lad dozing beside the cattle pen, while the blue bull was nowhere within it. The Monkey said, “Old sir, your bull has escaped! Your bull has escaped!” Greatly startled, Lord Lao said, “When did that wretched beast escape?” Amid the commotion, the lad finally awoke. He knelt before them and said, “Grand Master, your disciple fell asleep and does not know when it escaped.” Lord Lao cursed him. “How did you come to doze off?” The lad kowtowed and said, “Your disciple found an elixir pellet in the alchemy chamber. I ate it at once and then fell asleep here.” Lord Lao said, “It must have been one of the Sevenfold Refined Fire Elixirs made the other day. One pellet fell, and this wretch picked it up and ate it. Whoever takes one of those pellets sleeps for seven days. Seeing you asleep and itself unwatched, that wretched beast seized the chance to descend into the lower world. Today makes seven days indeed.”

p.src: He immediately checked whether any treasure had been stolen. The Monkey said, “I saw no particular treasure, only that he had a ring of tremendous power.” Lord Lao hastily inspected his possessions. Everything else was there; only the Diamond Snare was missing. Lord Lao said, “That wretched beast has stolen my Diamond Snare!” The Monkey said, “So that is what the treasure was! That was what struck me down before. He is now running wild in the lower world, and who knows how many of our things he has snared away?” Lord Lao asked, “Where is that wretched beast?” The Monkey replied, “He now dwells in Golden Pouch Cave on Golden Pouch Mountain. He captured my master, the Tang Monk, and took my Gold-Hooped Staff. When I called the heavenly troops to help, he also took the prince’s divine weapons. Then I summoned the Star Lord of Fire, and he took all his implements of fire as well. Only the Lord of the Waters, though unable to drown him, at least had none of his belongings taken. At last I appealed to the Tathagata, who sent arhats to cast cinnabar sand, but the monster took even their golden cinnabar sand. You, old sir, let this monster loose to rob and injure people. What punishment do you deserve?” Lord Lao said, “My Diamond Snare is the instrument I used when I passed through Hangu Pass and converted the Hu, a treasure I refined from my youth. No weapon whatsoever, nor water nor fire, can approach it. Had it stolen my plantain-leaf fan as well, even I could do nothing against it.”

p.src: The Monkey leaped down from the peak and again shouted abuse: “You bloated, accursed beast! Come out quickly and meet your death!” The little fiend went in once more to report. The old demon said, “Who knows whom that thieving monkey has invited this time?” He hastily snatched up his spear, took his treasure, and came out through the gate to confront him. The Monkey cursed him: “You vile demon, this time your death is certain! Do not run—take a blow from my palm!” He sprang forward until they were face-to-face, slapped the demon squarely across the cheek, then turned and fled. The demon whirled his spear and gave chase. Then a voice called from the high peak, “Bull, why have you not returned home? How much longer will you wait?” The demon raised his head and saw that it was the Most High Lord Lao. Terrified out of his wits, he said, “That thieving monkey truly is a demon at ferreting things out! How did he manage to track down my master?”

p.src: Lord Lao recited an incantation and waved his fan once. The monster threw his ring, but Lord Lao caught it neatly in one hand. He waved it again, and the monster’s strength ebbed and his sinews went numb. He resumed his true form, which proved to be a blue bull. Lord Lao breathed immortal breath upon the Diamond Snare and passed it through the monster’s nose. Taking off his robe sash, he tied it to the snare and held it as a lead. To this day there remains a ring for tethering a bull by the nose, also called a binlang; this is the origin of the term. Lord Lao took leave of the gods, mounted the blue bull, and rode a many-colored cloud straight back to Tushita Palace; having bound the monster, he ascended to the Heaven of Dissolving Hatred.

They readied the horse and luggage, and master and disciples left the cave, found the main road, and resumed their journey.

u.src: Only then did Great Sage Sun charge into the cave with the Heavenly King and the others. They killed all hundred or so lesser fiends and each recovered his weapons.

He thanked the Heavenly King and his sons, who returned to Heaven; the Duke of Thunder went back to his office, the Star Lord of Fire to his palace, the Lord of the Waters to his river, and the arhats westward.
Only afterward did he release the Tang Monk, Bajie, and Sha Monk and retrieve his iron staff.
The three thanked the Monkey once more. They readied the horse and luggage, and master and disciples left the cave, found the main road, and resumed their journey.

p.src: As they went along, they suddenly heard someone calling from beside the road, “Holy Monk of the Tang, come and eat a vegetarian meal before you go!” The elder monk was alarmed.

p.src: Who it was that called out remains unknown; listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
